opening: Attacks on Saudi Arabia pushed oil above $112 and prompted new evacuations, while Russia agreed in principle to resume three-way Ukraine talks even as missiles hit Kyiv. Typhoon Champi closed flights across Taiwan and Japan. In AI, Meta raised its spending ambitions and Anthropic launched a new agent app.

stories.threadTitle: The Iran war and Gulf security
stories.threadSummary: The widening conflict around Iran and its effects on Gulf states, shipping and energy infrastructure.
stories.title: Attacks reach deeper into Saudi Arabia as Aramco evacuates its headquarters
stories.body: Saudi Aramco told staff to leave its Dhahran headquarters and work remotely after attacks around eastern Saudi Arabia, Reuters reported, while the United States ordered some diplomatic staff and families out of the country. Houthi attacks killed people at King Fahd International Airport and near the Shaybah oilfield. Brent crude rose above $112 a barrel as traders priced a greater risk to Gulf energy infrastructure and shipping.
stories.whatChanged: The regional war is now disrupting the headquarters of the world's largest oil company and prompting US diplomatic evacuations in Saudi Arabia.
stories.whyMatters: Repeated strikes around Saudi energy and transport infrastructure raise the risk that the conflict affects physical oil operations rather than only prices and shipping expectations.
stories.uncertainty: Aramco did not publicly explain the reason for the Dhahran evacuation, and the operational effect on Saudi oil production was not established at the cutoff.
stories.watchNext: Whether Aramco reports production or export disruptions, whether Saudi retaliation expands, and whether further attacks reach airports, fields or export terminals.
keyFacts: Aramco instructed staff at its Dhahran headquarters to evacuate and work remotely on October 22
Two people were killed in the October 21 attack on King Fahd International Airport near Dammam, Reuters reported
Brent crude traded above $112 a barrel on October 22
The United States ordered some diplomatic staff and family members to leave Saudi Arabia

report.heading: What changed
paragraphs: Reuters reported that Saudi Aramco instructed staff at its Dhahran headquarters to evacuate and work remotely on Thursday, the first such evacuation there since the Iran war began. The move followed an attack on King Fahd International Airport near Dammam that killed two people and wounded eight. A separate Houthi drone attack aimed at the Shaybah oilfield also killed two people after interception by Saudi air defenses.

The headquarters itself had been struck earlier in October, causing extensive damage across several floors, according to people with direct knowledge cited by Reuters. The building contains an operations center used to oversee oil fields, refineries, terminals and pipelines. Aramco did not immediately explain Thursday's evacuation or report a production loss.

report.heading: Energy and diplomatic effects
paragraphs: Oil prices rose sharply as the attacks increased concern about supply from the world's most important exporting region. Reuters reported Brent above $112 a barrel, its highest level since May. The US State Department also ordered the departure of some diplomatic personnel and families from Saudi Arabia and other regional missions.

The price move reflects risk as well as confirmed disruption: there was no evidence by the cutoff of a broad Saudi production shutdown. That distinction matters because physical supply losses and precautionary evacuations have different implications for the duration of the shock.

report.heading: What comes next
paragraphs: Saudi Arabia has said it will defend its infrastructure and has struck Houthi missile sites. Egypt's president said his country would help defend Saudi territory if asked but ruled out offensive operations in Yemen. The next test is whether attacks continue against oil facilities and transport nodes, and whether Saudi or allied responses widen the conflict further.

stories.threadSummary: Russia's war on Ukraine, the diplomacy around it and its spillover into European security.
stories.title: Russia accepts new three-way Ukraine talks in principle as missiles hit Kyiv
stories.body: Russia agreed in principle to resume US-mediated technical talks with Ukraine after November 10, the Kremlin said after Steve Witkoff's nearly three-hour meeting with Vladimir Putin. The proposed talks would focus on postwar security for both countries. Hours later, Russian missiles struck Kyiv, killing two people and injuring more than 30, while Ukraine launched hundreds of drones toward Moscow. The diplomatic opening therefore arrived without a pause in the fighting.
stories.whatChanged: Putin moved from hearing the Oslo proposals to accepting a new round of three-way technical talks in principle, while overnight strikes underscored how far the sides remain from a ceasefire.
stories.whyMatters: The talks would be the first US-mediated three-way negotiations since February and could test whether the parties can move from competing ceasefire proposals to a security framework.
stories.uncertainty: No agreement on territory, ceasefire terms or security guarantees has been announced, and the Kremlin said the Oslo proposals contained little it considered useful.
stories.watchNext: Whether the proposed talks are formally scheduled after November 10, likely in Abu Dhabi, and whether Washington, Kyiv and Moscow agree on an agenda before then.
keyFacts: Russia said it was willing in principle to resume three-way talks after November 10
The Kremlin said the talks should focus on a post-conflict security system for Russia and Ukraine
Witkoff's meeting with Putin lasted almost three hours
Russian missiles struck Kyiv hours later, killing two people and injuring more than 30, according to Ukrainian reporting cited by the Financial Times

report.heading: A new negotiating round
paragraphs: Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said Putin told US envoy Steve Witkoff that Russia was willing in principle to resume talks next month with Ukraine and the United States. The proposed negotiations would be technical-level talks focused on a security system for both Russia and Ukraine after the conflict. Reuters reported that no such three-way talks have taken place since February.

Witkoff briefed Putin on the previous day's meeting in Oslo with Volodymyr Zelensky, the leaders of Norway and Finland and other European representatives. The Kremlin acknowledged new elements in those proposals but said they contained little it considered useful for resolving the war.

report.heading: Fighting continues
paragraphs: The diplomatic movement did not produce an immediate military pause. The Financial Times reported that Russian missiles hit Kyiv after the talks, killing two people and injuring more than 30 while damaging civilian infrastructure. Ukraine, meanwhile, sent hundreds of drones toward Moscow, disrupting airport operations.

The continued attacks are important context for the diplomatic headline: agreement to meet is not an agreement on a ceasefire, borders or guarantees. Kyiv continues to seek stronger air defenses and security commitments, while Moscow's conditions remain substantially different.

report.heading: What to watch
paragraphs: The Kremlin said talks could begin after November 10 and could take place in Abu Dhabi. The practical test will be whether all three governments confirm a venue, participants and a common agenda. Until then, the commitment is an opening for negotiations rather than evidence that a settlement is close.

stories.threadSummary: Typhoon Champi's path across the western Pacific and its effects on Taiwan, China and Japan.
stories.title: Typhoon Champi closes flights across Taiwan and Japan as its wind field expands
stories.body: Taiwan issued a land warning as Typhoon Champi approached with gusts above 227 kph and a wind field wide enough to cover most of the island. More than 200 flights were cancelled across Taiwan and Japan, northern Taiwan faced forecasts of nearly a metre of mountain rain, and Japan adjusted the multinational Keen Sword military exercise. The storm is expected to turn north toward southern Japan after passing Taiwan.
stories.whatChanged: Champi's expanding wind field brought most of Taiwan into its impact zone and began causing widespread travel and military-training disruptions before landfall or closest approach.
stories.whyMatters: The combination of extreme rain, high waves and a broad wind field means disruption extends well beyond the storm's center, including densely populated northern Taiwan and Japan's southern islands.
stories.uncertainty: The track and intensity can still shift; Taiwan had not ordered broad civilian evacuations by the cutoff.
stories.watchNext: Rainfall and landslide reports in northern Taiwan, the storm's turn toward the Chinese coast and Okinawa, and further transport cancellations.
keyFacts: Champi was about 520 km southeast of Taiwan's southern tip early October 22
Gusts exceeded 227 kph near the center
Its radius expanded to about 320 km
More than 200 flights were cancelled across Taiwan and Japan
Northern mountain areas of Taiwan could receive nearly one metre of rain

report.heading: Taiwan enters the storm's wind field
paragraphs: Taiwan's Central Weather Administration issued a land warning Thursday as Champi moved closer. Reuters reported that the storm, previously a super typhoon, had weakened somewhat but still carried gusts above 227 kph near its center. Its radius expanded to roughly 320 km, large enough for effects across most of Taiwan.

Authorities warned coastal communities about waves above six metres and forecast close to a metre of rain in northern mountain areas. President Lai Ching-te urged people to stay away from coasts and mountains. Taiwan cancelled 125 mostly domestic flights, while rail services were still operating at the time of the report.

report.heading: Japan and the regional path
paragraphs: Japan cancelled more than 100 domestic flights scheduled between Thursday and Sunday, affecting more than 11,000 passengers. The storm also forced daily adjustments to Keen Sword, a large US-Japan military exercise involving about 56,000 personnel and participants from several allied countries.

Forecasts had Champi passing northeast of Taiwan, bending toward the Chinese coast and then moving toward southern Japan. Because the storm remains large, places outside the center line can still experience dangerous rain, wind and surf.

stories.threadSummary: Protests, riots and the French government's response during the 2026 political and cost-of-living crisis.
stories.title: Macron tightens protest restrictions ahead of another volatile weekend
stories.body: President Emmanuel Macron said authorities would ban what he called illegitimate protests while allowing union-organized demonstrations, sometimes on altered routes to protect businesses. Lyon banned all Saturday protests as cities prepared for fresh demonstrations after the previous weekend's riots and looting. The government blamed ultra-left groups for violence; opposition figures disputed attempts to assign responsibility broadly.
stories.whatChanged: France moved from emergency policing after last weekend's unrest to broader preventive restrictions on demonstrations planned for the coming days.

sources.title: France's Macron tightens curbs on protests, blaming hard left for unrest

stories.threadSummary: How companies are changing staffing and operations as AI tools move into routine work.
stories.title: Barclays says it will cut 5,000 jobs as AI and automation lower fixed costs
stories.body: Barclays said it expects to eliminate about 5,000 jobs, roughly 5% of its workforce, during 2026 as it uses AI and other technology to reduce fixed costs. About 1,000 cuts have already occurred and another 4,000 are planned by year-end. The bank said support roles, including developers, account for much of the reduction.
stories.whatChanged: A major European bank attached a concrete workforce reduction to its use of AI and automation rather than describing the technology only as a future efficiency target.

sources.title: Barclays to slash 5,000 jobs in AI-powered cost-cutting drive

stories.threadSummary: Wildfires, haze and the response across Indonesia during the 2026 fire season.
stories.title: Indonesia says fire hotspots are easing, but rain is still not enough
stories.body: Indonesia's disaster agency said wildfire hotspots declined over the past week but the country remained on high alert because sporadic rain had not extinguished fires. Haze continued in parts of Borneo, where students protested the government's handling of the crisis. Authorities warned that conditions could worsen again if rainfall remains insufficient.
stories.whatChanged: The number of hotspots fell, but officials said the improvement was not yet enough to end the wildfire emergency or haze risk.

sources.title: Indonesia's fire hotspots ease but rain still not enough, official says

stories.threadSummary: The capital, chips and data centers being committed to build and run frontier AI systems.
stories.title: Meta raises the floor on its AI spending as Muse passes 10 million users
stories.body: Meta reported quarterly revenue of $64.6 billion and raised the lower end of its 2026 capital-spending range to $135 billion, while saying its Muse AI agent had passed 10 million users. The company also approved a new class of non-voting shares, giving it another financing tool as AI infrastructure costs rise. Strong adoption is therefore arriving alongside an unusually large and still-growing capital commitment.
stories.whatChanged: Meta paired early evidence of mass-market agent adoption with a higher spending floor and a new financing structure for its AI expansion.
stories.whyMatters: The numbers make Meta a useful test of whether consumer AI agents can generate enough durable value to justify hyperscale infrastructure spending.
stories.hook: Muse's adoption is becoming measurable; so is the extraordinary cost of serving and improving it.
stories.uncertainty: User counts do not establish sustained engagement or profitability, and Meta has not shown that Muse's direct economics cover its compute costs.
stories.watchNext: Muse engagement and paid conversion, Meta's 2027 capital-spending guidance, and whether the new share class is used for financing or acquisitions.
keyFacts: Meta reported $64.6 billion in third-quarter revenue
Muse passed 10 million users, according to Meta
Meta's 2026 capital-expenditure range is $135 billion to $145 billion
Meta approved a new class of non-voting shares

report.heading: Adoption meets infrastructure cost
paragraphs: Meta's third-quarter results put two sides of the AI race in the same set of numbers. Revenue rose to $64.6 billion, while the company said Muse, its consumer AI agent, had passed 10 million users. Meta also lifted the lower end of its annual capital-expenditure guidance to $135 billion, leaving the top at $145 billion.

The company approved a new class of non-voting stock that can be used for financing, acquisitions and employee compensation without changing voting control in the same way ordinary shares would. The move gives Meta additional flexibility while it funds data centers, chips and model development.

report.heading: What the user number does and does not show
paragraphs: Ten million users is evidence that an agent capable of carrying out tasks can attract a large audience quickly. It is not yet evidence that the product is profitable. Compute-intensive agents can be expensive to serve, and adoption figures alone do not show how frequently people use Muse, how many pay, or whether transaction-based revenue will offset inference costs.

That makes Meta's next disclosures unusually informative. If engagement and monetization rise while compute efficiency improves, the economics of consumer agents look stronger; if spending continues to outrun direct returns, the gap becomes harder to ignore.

sources.title: Meta Q3 revenue tops estimates and Zuckerberg says Muse accounts have topped 10 million

stories.threadSummary: The move from chatbots toward AI systems that can carry out multi-step work for users.
stories.title: Anthropic launches Claude Duet as a standalone agent for delegated work
stories.body: Anthropic launched Claude Duet, a standalone agent application aimed at professionals and small businesses. Rather than waiting for a sequence of prompts, the product is designed to take delegated tasks and carry them through with greater autonomy. The release extends the industry's shift from conversational assistants toward software expected to act across work processes, where reliability, permissions and oversight become as important as model quality.
stories.whatChanged: Anthropic moved its agent strategy into a dedicated product intended for proactive, delegated work rather than only conversational assistance.
stories.whyMatters: Standalone agents put model capabilities into longer real-world action loops, making practical reliability and human control more consequential than benchmark performance alone.
stories.hook: The competition is moving from who has the best chatbot to who can be trusted to carry out work.
stories.uncertainty: The launch announcement does not by itself establish how reliably Duet completes long tasks or how users will manage mistakes and permissions at scale.
stories.watchNext: Independent testing of task completion, permission controls and failure recovery, plus adoption among businesses that give the agent access to real workflows.
keyFacts: Anthropic announced Claude Duet on October 21
Duet is a standalone AI agent application
Anthropic is positioning it for professionals and small-business owners
The product is designed to complete delegated tasks on a user's behalf

report.heading: A product built around delegation
paragraphs: Anthropic announced Claude Duet as a standalone application centered on agentic work. Reuters described the product as a proactive assistant for professionals and small-business owners that can complete tasks on a user's behalf. The distinction is less about a new chat interface than about how much of a workflow the system is expected to carry without step-by-step prompting.

That puts Duet into the same broader contest as other general-purpose agents from major AI companies. The competitive question is increasingly whether an assistant can operate usefully across real tools and processes, not only whether it can produce a strong answer in a single conversation.

report.heading: Why reliability becomes the central test
paragraphs: Longer action chains compound errors. An agent that can send, change or submit things on a user's behalf needs clear permissions, good recovery from mistakes and enough transparency for a person to know what happened. Those properties are difficult to infer from a launch announcement.

Duet is therefore significant as a product-direction signal, while its practical importance will depend on independent use. Evidence to watch includes completion rates on real tasks, the frequency and cost of human intervention, and how the system behaves when instructions conflict or external tools fail.

sources.title: Anthropic unveils Claude Duet AI agent app
